planting.note: Divide and transplant as new shoots emerge in spring; established clumps resent root disturbance.

directions: This southeastern Chinese toad lily was only formally separated from the similar Tricyrtis macropoda in 2001, and it grows noticeably taller and more robust, with larger leaves and a rhizome that is renewed annually rather than persisting from year to year. In late summer and fall it produces an unusually heavy show of flowers, sometimes over fifty per stem, each white to pale yellow and heavily freckled with small purple-red spots. Grow it in humus-rich, evenly moist woodland soil in dappled to full shade, mimicking the understory forests of Anhui, Fujian, Guangdong, Guangxi, Hunan, Jiangxi, and Zhejiang where it occurs naturally. Mulch the crowns over winter in the cooler end of its range, since the renewable rhizome is somewhat less cold-hardy than that of the long-cultivated Japanese toad lily species.
